summary:
Magdalena department stands under the national framework of Colombia, where legal gender recognition has rested on self-recognition since Constitutional Court jurisprudence of 1993 and, since a rule change approved in June 2015, has required only a signed declaration before a notary. The earlier route, in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments, no longer applies. Same-sex marriage has been available since April 2016, full adoption rights for same-sex couples since 2015, and national identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025. Trans Colombians have been permitted to serve openly in the armed forces since 2015.

No finding specific to Magdalena on law, enforcement practice, facilities or incidents affecting trans people appears in the sourced material; two of the four sources state the absence directly. The risk picture for a visitor to the department is therefore drawn from the national record.

That record documents sustained lethal violence. An investigation published on 30 July 2024 recorded 41 trans women killed in Colombia during 2023 and a further eight between February and April 2024. The Attorney General's Office registered 35 LGBTI murders between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025.

Individual cases show the pattern in ordinary urban settings as well as under armed-group control. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia in April 2025; a video of the assault circulated from 5 April showing her with fractured limbs in a creek, before she drowned. President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities.

The institutional response lags the violence. An activist quoted in the July 2024 investigation stated that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that rising killings must be addressed urgently.
tangentialFactors:
The sharpest documented violence risk sits where armed groups operate. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns announced through flyers targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and gave trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed; in Guajira, flyers posted from March 2024 carried a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". Caquetá and Guajira stand as examples of a pattern reported across territories under armed-group control, and none of this reporting is Magdalena-specific.

Some conflict-era violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against them constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern.

Colombian society is described in the sourced material as generally conservative on LGBT issues. An Invamer poll of October 2019 recorded 50% support for same-sex marriage for the first time, with 47% opposed. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025, so the protections a visitor relies on rest on existing statute and court jurisprudence rather than a single consolidated statute.
localsOnly:
For residents of Magdalena, changing the sex marker on government-issued identification is an administrative act: a document signed before a notary, with no surgical requirement, psychiatric evaluation or physical examination. Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 grounds the right in self-recognition.

Consensual same-sex activity has been legal nationally since 1981, and Congress passed a law banning discrimination based on sexual orientation in 2011. Same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015 and have been able to marry since April 2016, and trans people have been able to serve openly in the military since 2015.

Courts have intervened directly in detention. A Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system, a protection available to residents of the department as well as to visitors.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether armed-group threats, kill lists or "social cleansing" campaigns operate within Magdalena is unresolved in the sourced material; the documented cases come from Caquetá, Guajira and Antioquia, and no Magdalena-specific reporting was available.

Recognition of transfemicide by prosecutors handling cases in Magdalena is unresolved. The sourced material records an activist's statement that the prosecutor's office does not recognise the offence nationally, without department-level detail.

Facilities, service access and care provision for trans people in Magdalena, including gender-affirming healthcare and the availability of non-binary identification markers at local registration offices, are not sourced and remain open questions.

The passage of the comprehensive trans law under legislative consideration in 2025 is unresolved in the sources, which describe it as pending rather than enacted or defeated.
